description: Somos estudiantes de distintas carreras con un interés en común: las matemáticas, la estadística, la probabilidad y la inteligencia artificial. Nos gusta la tecnología y aprender cosas nuevas, y este reto nos pareció una buena oportunidad para aplicar lo que sabemos a problemas reales.
summary: Expediente Tierra lets anyone pick a place on Earth, a country, or the whole planet and find out what's changing there: which variable, where, by how much, and whether it's significant or not. It pulls 46 variables from NASA POWER and Google Earth Engine, then runs five significance tests corrected for autocorrelation. That matters: the standard Mann-Kendall test flagged fake trends up to 64% of the time on our simulated data. Ours: 3–4%. It runs in English and Spanish.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?

Pick a place, a country, or the whole planet, and Expediente Tierra tells you what's changing there, where, by how much, and whether it's real. It pulls 46 variables from NASA POWER and Google Earth Engine, removes the seasonal cycle, maps the trend cell by cell, and runs five significance tests corrected for autocorrelation. You get a rate of change, its uncertainty, a level of evidence, and a downloadable report, in English or Spanish.

What benefits does it have?

It tells you how much to trust a trend. On our simulated data, the classic Mann-Kendall test invented trends up to 64% of the time; ours, 3–4%, while still catching 79–98% of real ones. Our New Delhi groundwater result (3.8 cm/year lost) matches a published Nature study (4.0 ± 1.0).

What is the intended impact of the project?

Anyone, from a student to a local government, can ask "is my region really warming or drying out?" and get an honest answer, including "not enough evidence yet." Many climate claims rest on a chart that goes up; this tool lets people check them.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?

Python with Streamlit, Plotly, pandas, NumPy, and SciPy; the NASA POWER API and Google Earth Engine; GitHub and 68 automated tests; a MacBook. Claude (Anthropic) helped us write the code. The app itself uses no AI, so every result is a reproducible calculation.

How is your project creative?

It measures its own error rate and lets you watch it: the Laboratory page generates trend-free data live and shows the classic test raising false alarms while ours doesn't. It also splits trends by month, cross-checks a second data source, and runs the same tests on a single point, a whole country, or the entire globe.

What factors did your team consider?

Data quality first: we screened every variable at seven sites and dropped or trimmed the ones with satellite artifacts. Then statistical honesty: we correct for autocorrelation and multiple testing, and say "insufficient evidence" when that's the truth. We also wrote for students (simple definitions, two languages), stated our limits openly, and declared and verified every piece of AI-assisted work.
